messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. James Johnson is a 68-year-old widowed African American Policy Analyst who recently experienced a life-threatening illness that has left him grappling with significant psychological distress. His experience of nearly losing his life to a serious medical condition has profoundly impacted his daily functioning and emotional well-being. James recounts the moment he first learned about his diagnosis, feeling an overwhelming sense of fear and helplessness. The hospitalization was marked by intense anxiety and physical discomfort that he could barely tolerate. He had difficulty concentrating during his stay in the intensive care unit (ICU), where every sound amplified his sense of danger. This acute awareness of potential threats continued even after his discharge, leaving him feeling constantly tense and ready to react to any perceived threat. James's experience with the life-threatening illness has led to fragmented memories that feel disconnected from his present self. At times, he can recall specific moments during his hospital stay but feels completely numb, as if it happened to someone else. These emotions of detachment are often punctuated by intrusive recollections where the memory seems to be happening in the present rather than something that is over. When these memories return, they overwhelm him with such intensity that he has to stop whatever he is doing and retreat into a state of numbness. His negative appraisals about his body and emotions have become central to his distress. James believes that he will never be able to feel normal emotions again and feels betrayed by his own body, which continues to react as if he were still in danger even when he is safe at home. He has come to trust neither his body nor the world around him, leading to a persistent state of alertness and tension. The belief that his body cannot be trusted exacerbates his feelings of constant threat. James feels on guard even inside his own home, believing that any physical sensation could signal another medical emergency. This heightened sense of danger is further fueled by the vivid recollections of his illness, which seem to replay in real-time, causing him intense emotional distress and reinforcing his negative appraisals about his body’s reliability. James's occupation as a Policy Analyst has been significantly impacted by these symptoms. He often finds it difficult to concentrate on work-related tasks, leading to mistakes that he fears will jeopardize his job security. His colleagues have noticed changes in his behavior; he is more withdrawn and less engaged in team discussions, which he once enjoyed. The cycle of threat and distress has become self-reinforcing for James. The overwhelming memories intensify his feelings of constant danger, while his negative appraisals further fuel this sense of threat. As a result, he lives in a state of persistent vigilance, unable to fully relax or engage with the world around him. What finally brought James to seek help was a recent incident where he experienced a sudden onset of symptoms at work, causing significant distress and concern among his colleagues. He is most afraid of losing control over his life and being debilitated by these overwhelming feelings. At the same time, he is hopeful that with support, he can regain some semblance of normalcy and reconnect with the world around him. James's current state reflects a profound struggle to navigate daily life while grappling with intense psychological distress. His journey toward recovery will likely require addressing both his intrusive memories and negative appraisals in order to break the cycle of threat and reactivity that has become central to his experience.
